page: Vultr vhp-2c-4gb-amd is a High Performance family virtual machine powered by an AMD EPYC processor using the x86_64 architecture. It features 2 shared vCPUs mapped to 1 physical core with 2 threads per core, operating at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz. The processor includes 32 KB of L1d cache, 0.5 MB of L2 cache, and 16 MB of L3 cache, with support for AVX, AES, SHA_NI, and BMI2 instruction sets. The instance is equipped with 4.0 GB of system memory, providing 2.0 GB per core, and includes 100 GB of local NVMe SSD storage along with one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Performance benchmarks indicate average single-core capabilities but weaker multi-core and memory performance. The stress-ng single-core CPU test achieved a score of 2318.46, placing it in the average tier, while the multi-core score of 4565.57 falls into the lower quartile. Memory bandwidth is limited, with read-only large block speeds at 25.27 GB/sec and write speeds at 21.3 GB/sec. Complex operations show constraints, as evidenced by a Geekbench clang software compilation score of 2420.0 and a Passmark database operations score of 600.44, both of which rank in the bottom tier.

Given its shared CPU allocation and modest memory capacity, this server offers a highly cost-efficient entry point for workloads that do not require sustained, high-density compute resources. It is suitable for lightweight applications such as basic web serving, small-scale development environments, simple text processing, and low-traffic utility services. However, the shared CPU model and lower multi-threaded performance make it less suitable for intensive database operations, heavy compilation tasks, or memory-bound workloads.
description: Vultr vhp-2c-4gb-amd is an entry-level virtual machine from the High Performance family, featuring 2 shared vCPUs on an AMD EPYC x86_64 processor with a 2.0 GHz clock speed. It is configured with 4.0 GB of RAM and 100 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. While single-core performance is average, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2318.46, multi-core and memory benchmarks are generally weak, as shown by a Geekbench multi-core score of 2253.0 and a Passmark memory score of 1171.74. This shared-resource configuration provides a highly cost-effective option for low-intensity workloads. It is best suited for lightweight web serving, utility tasks, and development environments that do not demand sustained multi-threaded compute or high memory bandwidth.
